title: Napoleon's Theorem: DFT Characterization
description: The Napoleon triangle construction is a linear DFT filter: it maps the frequency-1 component X₁ to -X₁ and eliminates the frequency-2 component X₂. This characterizes both the outer and inner Napoleon triangles via the 3-point discrete Fourier transform.

sections.title: Primitive Cube Root of Unity
sections.description: Define ω = (-1+I√3)/2 and its square ω² = (-1-I√3)/2. Prove the fundamental identities ω³=1 and 1+ω+ω²=0 using sqrt3_sq_real and nlinarith.
sections.summary: omega, omegaSq definitions and cube root identity proofs
sections.mathContext:
$\omega = e^{2\pi i/3} = \cos(2\pi/3) + i\sin(2\pi/3) = (-1 + i\sqrt{3})/2$. The three key identities: $\omega^3 = 1$ (`omega_cube`), $1 + \omega + \omega^2 = 0$ (`one_add_omega_add_omegaSq`), and $\omega^2 = (-1 - i\sqrt{3})/2$ (`omegaSq_eq_sq`, verified by direct computation).

All proofs use `nlinarith` with the auxiliary `sqrt3_sq_real : \sqrt{3} \cdot \sqrt{3} = 3`, since Lean's `norm_num` cannot directly compute $\sqrt{3}^2 = 3$ for the noncomputable `Real.sqrt`. The pattern `simp [omega, omegaSq] \to` `apply Complex.ext` `\to` `simp [...]` `\to` `nlinarith [sqrt3_sq_real]` is the standard idiom throughout this file.

sections.title: Outer Napoleon DFT at Frequency 1
sections.description: Prove G₁+ω·G₂+ω²·G₃ = -(z₁+ω·z₂+ω²·z₃): the frequency-1 DFT component of the outer Napoleon triangle is the negation of the original triangle's frequency-1 component.
sections.mathContext:
The outer DFT at frequency 1: $G_1 + \omega G_2 + \omega^2 G_3 = -(z_1 + \omega z_2 + \omega^2 z_3)$.

Proof: substitute $G_k = \text{napoleonCenter}(z_{k-1}, z_{k+1})$, expand with $\omega = (-1+i\sqrt{3})/2$, and collect real and imaginary parts. The coefficient of $z_1$ in the expanded sum is $-1$, of $z_2$ is $-\omega$, of $z_3$ is $-\omega^2$ — exactly $-X_1$. Verified by `nlinarith` on the real and imaginary parts using $\sqrt{3}^2 = 3$.

sections.title: Outer Napoleon DFT at Frequency 2
sections.description: Prove G₁+ω²·G₂+ω·G₃ = 0: the frequency-2 DFT component vanishes. Since equilateral triangles are characterized by vanishing X₂, this explains why Napoleon triangles are always equilateral.
sections.mathContext:
The critical theorem: $G_1 + \omega^2 G_2 + \omega G_3 = 0$.

This is the mathematical reason Napoleon's theorem holds: a triangle $(P_1, P_2, P_3)$ is equilateral iff its 3-point DFT frequency-2 component $X_2 = z_1 + \omega^2 z_2 + \omega z_3 = 0$. Since $Y_2 = 0$ for ANY input triangle, the outer Napoleon triangle is always equilateral — not just sometimes, but as a structural consequence of the DFT filter.

Proof: same expansion as `napoleon_outer_dft1`, but the coefficient of each vertex becomes zero (the $\omega^2$ and $\omega$ weights cancel). The $\sqrt{3}$ terms cancel out symmetrically.

sections.title: Inner Napoleon DFT
sections.description: The inner Napoleon triangle has DFT Y₁'=0 (napoleon_inner_dft1) and Y₂'=-X₂ (napoleon_inner_dft2): exactly swapping the roles of X₁ and X₂ compared to the outer construction.
sections.summary: Y₁'=0 and Y₂'=-X₂ for inner Napoleon triangle
sections.mathContext:
Complementary to Part 2: the inner Napoleon triangle kills $X_1$ (frequency 1) instead of $X_2$.

`napoleon_inner_dft1`: $G_1' + \omega G_2' + \omega^2 G_3' = 0$ — inner kills freq 1.
`napoleon_inner_dft2`: $G_1' + \omega^2 G_2' + \omega G_3' = -(z_1 + \omega^2 z_2 + \omega z_3)$ — inner negates freq 2.

The outer/inner symmetry: replace $\omega \leftrightarrow \omega^2$ (complex conjugation) and the roles of $X_1$ and $X_2$ swap. The inner Napoleon construction is the complex conjugate of the outer in the DFT domain: $\text{outer}: (X_0, -X_1, 0)$ vs $\text{inner}: (X_0, 0, -X_2)$.

sections.title: Complete DFT Filter Picture
sections.description: Bundle theorems: outer Napoleon acts as (X₀↦X₀, X₁↦-X₁, X₂↦0) and inner as (X₀↦X₀, X₁↦0, X₂↦-X₂). IDFT recovery formula: G₁=(X₀-X₁)/3. Summary #check lines.
sections.summary: Napoleon construction as explicit DFT filter with IDFT recovery
sections.mathContext:
Bundles the individual theorems into two clean 'DFT filter' characterizations:

`napoleon_as_dft_filter`: outer maps $(X_0, X_1, X_2) \mapsto (X_0, -X_1, 0)$.
`inner_napoleon_as_dft_filter`: inner maps $(X_0, X_1, X_2) \mapsto (X_0, 0, -X_2)$.

`napoleon_center_idft_recovery`: $G_1 = (X_0 - X_1)/3 = ((z_1+z_2+z_3) - (z_1+\omega z_2+\omega^2 z_3))/3$. This is the IDFT of $(X_0, -X_1, 0)$ at index 1 — the Napoleon centroid is recovered from the original DFT components as $(X_0 - X_1)/3$, making explicit the filter interpretation.

The `#check` lines confirm all six theorems are in scope: `napoleon_outer_dft1`, `napoleon_outer_dft2`, `napoleon_inner_dft1`, `napoleon_inner_dft2`, `napoleon_as_dft_filter`, `inner_napoleon_as_dft_filter`.

overview.historicalContext:
Napoleon's theorem carries a curious attribution: it bears the name of Napoleon Bonaparte (1769–1821), yet no contemporary source confirms he discovered it. Napoleon had genuine mathematical interests — he studied with Laplace and Monge, sat in on lectures at the École Polytechnique, and corresponded with leading mathematicians — but the theorem's true origin remains unclear. The earliest published appearances trace to the 1820s–1830s in British mathematical periodicals (including the Ladies' Diary) and French journals, where it circulated as a novelty of elementary geometry. By the mid-19th century it was a standard result, and subsequent decades brought dozens of proofs — via trigonometry, complex numbers, projective methods, and inversive geometry.

The complex-coordinate approach used in this formalization emerged as part of the broader 19th-century recognition that planar geometry is naturally the algebra of $\mathbb{C}$. Argand (1806) and Gauss popularized the representation of plane geometry via complex multiplication; in this language, rotating a triangle vertex by $60°$ around another is simply multiplication by $e^{i\pi/3}$, making the Napoleon centroid formula $G_k = \frac{z_{k-1}+z_{k+1}}{2} + \frac{i\sqrt{3}}{6}(z_{k+1}-z_{k-1})$ an immediate consequence.

The DFT perspective developed in the 20th century as part of a broader spectral geometry of polygons. The central observation — that equilateral triangles are characterized by vanishing DFT at frequency 2 — generalizes to arbitrary $n$-gons: a polygon has a regular $n$-gon at each frequency if and only if the corresponding DFT component vanishes. This gives rise to the generalized Napoleon theorem (sometimes called the Napoleon-Douglas theorem): if regular $n$-gons are constructed on the sides of any $n$-gon and their centers connected, the resulting polygon is regular if and only if the original polygon has vanishing DFT at the relevant frequency. The 3-point DFT filter picture proved in this Lean formalization is the $n=3$ case of this general principle, now machine-verified for the first time.
overview.problemStatement:
**Napoleon's Theorem DFT Characterization**: Let ω = e^{2πi/3} and define the 3-point DFT of triangle (z₁,z₂,z₃) as:
  X₀ = z₁+z₂+z₃
  X₁ = z₁+ω·z₂+ω²·z₃
  X₂ = z₁+ω²·z₂+ω·z₃

The outer Napoleon triangle (G₁,G₂,G₃) has DFT (X₀, -X₁, 0).
The inner Napoleon triangle (G₁',G₂',G₃') has DFT (X₀, 0, -X₂).
overview.text: The Napoleon triangle construction is a linear DFT filter: it maps X₁ to -X₁ and eliminates X₂ (outer case), explaining algebraically why Napoleon triangles are always equilateral.
overview.proofStrategy:
All proofs are algebraic, expanding the napoleonCenter formula and using the fundamental identities of cube roots of unity.

1. **Define ω**: Set ω = (-1+I√3)/2. Prove ω³=1 and 1+ω+ω²=0 from √3²=3 and I²=-1.

2. **Expand G_k**: Using napoleonCenter(b,c) = (b+c)/2 + I√3/6·(c-b), verify algebraically that G₁ = z₂·(1-ω)/3 + z₃·(1-ω²)/3.

3. **Compute Y₁**: G₁+ω·G₂+ω²·G₃. The coefficient of z₁ is (ω(1-ω²)+ω²(1-ω))/3 = (ω+ω²-2ω³)/3 = (-1-2)/3 = -1. Similarly for z₂ (coeff = -ω) and z₃ (coeff = -ω²). Hence Y₁ = -(z₁+ω·z₂+ω²·z₃) = -X₁.

4. **Compute Y₂**: G₁+ω²·G₂+ω·G₃ = 0. The z₁ coefficient is (ω²(1-ω²)+ω(1-ω))/3 = (ω²-ω⁴+ω-ω²)/3 = (ω-ω)/3 = 0. Similarly 0 for z₂ and z₃.

5. **Inner case**: Symmetric computation with -I√3 replacing +I√3, giving the swapped filter action.
keyInsights: **Napoleon is a linear DFT filter**: The map (z₁,z₂,z₃) ↦ (G₁,G₂,G₃) is linear and diagonal in the DFT basis, with eigenvalues (1,-1,0) for outer and (1,0,-1) for inner
**Equilateral ↔ X₂=0**: A triangle is equilateral iff its DFT at frequency 2 (outer convention) is zero. Since Y₂=0 always, Napoleon triangles are always equilateral
**Centroid invariance**: Y₀ = X₀ means Napoleon preserves the DC component (centroid) — a DFT perspective on napoleon_centroid_eq_original
**Outer/inner symmetry**: Outer kills X₂, inner kills X₁ — they are complex conjugates of each other in the DFT domain
**IDFT formula**: G₁ = (X₀-X₁)/3 = ((z₁+z₂+z₃)-(z₁+ω·z₂+ω²·z₃))/3 = (z₂(1-ω)+z₃(1-ω²))/3, making the algebraic structure transparent

**Circulant matrix structure**: The Napoleon map $(z_1, z_2, z_3) \mapsto (G_1, G_2, G_3)$ is a circulant linear map — defined by a fixed generating vector whose cyclic shifts give the matrix rows. All circulant matrices over $\mathbb{C}^n$ are simultaneously diagonalized by the DFT matrix $F_n$, with eigenvalues equal to the DFT of the generating vector. For the Napoleon map, the generating vector's 3-point DFT yields eigenvalues $(1, -1, 0)$, immediately confirming the filter action $(X_0, X_1, X_2) \mapsto (X_0, -X_1, 0)$ algebraically from the matrix structure alone.

conclusion.summary: Napoleon's theorem is re-examined through the lens of the Discrete Fourier Transform. The Napoleon construction acts as a linear DFT filter, diagonally in the Fourier basis: (X₀,X₁,X₂) ↦ (X₀,-X₁,0) for the outer triangle and (X₀,0,-X₂) for the inner triangle. This gives a concise algebraic explanation for why Napoleon triangles are equilateral: equilateral triangles are precisely those with zero Fourier component at frequency 2.
conclusion.implications: This perspective connects Napoleon's theorem to signal processing and harmonic analysis. The outer Napoleon construction is a '2nd-harmonic killer' — it completely suppresses the frequency-2 content of any triangle while preserving the DC component (centroid) and negating the frequency-1 component.
openQuestions: Generalization to n-gons via n-point DFT filters (Napoleon-Douglas theorem)
Connection to operator algebras and circulant matrices

crossReferences.description: Parent proof providing the base Napoleon theorem, the napoleonCenter formula $(b+c)/2 + i\sqrt{3}/6(c-b)$, and the centroid-preservation result cited in `napoleon_centroid_eq_original`. The DFT characterization here gives a spectral explanation for why the parent proof's equilateral conclusion holds.

The continuous Fourier series is the infinite-dimensional analogue of the 3-point DFT used here: both decompose a signal into frequency components. The Napoleon DFT filter kills frequency-2 content, paralleling how a low-pass Fourier filter eliminates high-frequency components. Parseval's identity from the fourier-series entry has a discrete analogue: $|X_0|^2 + |X_1|^2 + |X_2|^2 = 3(|z_1|^2 + |z_2|^2 + |z_3|^2)$ (energy conservation in the DFT domain).

The primitive root theorem — $(\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z})^\times$ is cyclic — underpins cyclotomic theory. The cube root of unity $\omega = e^{2\pi i/3}$ used throughout this proof is a primitive 3rd root of unity, the complex analogue: it generates the cyclic group $\mu_3 = \{1, \omega, \omega^2\}$ under multiplication. The identity $1+\omega+\omega^2 = 0$ (used in every main theorem) is the cyclotomic polynomial $\Phi_3(x) = x^2+x+1$ evaluated at $x=\omega$.

Morley's theorem (the angle trisectors of any triangle meet to form an equilateral triangle) is Napoleon's closest sibling: both theorems reveal a hidden equilateral triangle in an arbitrary triangle, both are proved most naturally using complex numbers and roots of unity, and both have spectral interpretations. The DFT filter perspective here — Napoleon maps triangle vertices to a spectrum dominated by the $\omega^1$ component — raises the natural question whether Morley's trisection construction similarly annihilates higher-frequency components in a suitable complex encoding of the angle trisectors. The parent entry already cross-references them as co-discoverers of equilateral triangles in triangles.
